Judgment

1. This order shall decide an appeal filed under Section 70 of Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006 (hereinafter referred to "FSS Act") assailing the impugned order dated 02.06.2021 passed by the Ld.
Adjudicating Officer (ADM), District East, Delhi in the case title Food Safety Officer v. Shiv Kumar Goel & Others, imposing a penalty of Rs.10,000/ each upon appellant nos.1,2&3 and Rs.20,000/
each upon appellant nos. 4,5&6 under Section 52 of FSS Act.

entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text:
2. The facts giving rise to the present case are that the sample of "Bhujia" were taken by the Food Safety Officer (hereinafter referred to 'FSO'), which consisted of four sealed packets of 400 grams,
having identical label & declaration for analysis on 11.10.2018 from M/s Aggarwal Super Store situated at C19/54, Nehru Market, Kalyanpuri, Delhi91, which is the proprietorship concern of appellant no.2 and was being marketed by appellant Shiv Kumar Goel (appellant no.1).

A fortiori there are no question raised as about the procedural compliance committed by the FSO and suffice to state that one counterpart of the sample was sent to Food Analyst, Government of Delhi laboratory situated at Lawrence Road, Industrial Area, Delhi, which after analysis vide report dated 25.10.2018 brought out that the sample was "misbranded" on account of violation of Rules 2.2.2.2(c), 2.2.2.5(ii)(b) and 2.2.2.10 of the Food Safety & Standards (Packaging & Labelling)
Regulation, 2011 (hereinafter referred to "FSSPL Regulation, 2011"),

since the name of the specific 'edible oil' was not declared in the list of ingredients besides not mentioning or declaring the type of flavouring agent as per Regulation 2.2.2.5(ii)(b) of FSSPL Regulation, 2011; and as also holding that the "best before date" was not declared as per Regulation 2.2.2.10 of FSSPL Regulation, 2011.
Accordingly, the Ld. Adjudicating Officer after holding inquiry imposed the aforementioned fine/penalty in terms of Section 52 of the FSS Act.

3. On filing of the present appeal, the operation of the impugned order was stayed by the Ld.
Predecessor of this court (as his lordship was then) vide order dated 23.07.2021 subject to furnishing of the DD/FDR/Bank Guarantee for the amount equivalent to the penalty/fine imposed by the Ld. Adjudicating Officer, which was complied with.

4. Notice has been issued to the respondent/State and a reply has been filed, to which a rejoinder was also filed and the narratives of the same are not mentioned for the sake of brevity since the present appeal pertains to only raising of a legal issue with no denial on factual aspects.

sentences.text: In short, the appellants have assailed the impugned order primarily on the grounds that the Delhi Laboratory was not competent as per Section 43 of FSS Act; and that the Adjudicating Officer failed to appreciate the order dated 17.07.2018, followed by another clarification dated 17.01.2020 and Section 16(5) of FSS Act enjoins upon the Food Authority to issue "improvement notices" for such minor labeling violations instead of launching reckless prosecution; and lastly that Adjudicating Authority failed to appreciate that sampled commodity i.e. Bhujia was manufactured by respondent nos. 4,5&6 and was supplied to them against valid invoices and therefore, the Adjudicating Authority should have accorded benefit to the appellants in terms of Section 80(B)(2)(a) of FSS Act.
DECISION 6.
I have given my anxious consideration to the rival submissions advanced at the bar.
I have gone through the record of Ld. Adjudicating Officer and the record of the present appeal and documents filed therewith.
7. Ld.

Counsel for the appellant has relied upon the decision in R. Chandershekhran & Anr. v. State of Madras 2017(1) FAC 88 and M/s Nestle India Ltd v. Food Safety and Standards Authority of India and Ors. 2015(2) FAC 56.

entities.text: R. Chandershekhran & Anr. v. State of Madras 2017(1) FAC 88
entities.label: PRECEDENT

entities.text: M/s Nestle India Ltd v. Food Safety and Standards Authority of India and Ors. 2015(2) FAC 56
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: I have gone the proposition of law laid down in the said two cases as well.
8. In order to decide the present appeal, it would be expedient to refer to the main provisions of the FSS Act which come into play in the matter before us.

Section 3(zf) of FSS Act defines "misbranded food" to means an article of food which is offered or promoted for sale with false, misleading or deceptive claims upon the label of the package and the punishment is provided under Section 52 of the FSS Act.

Further, Section 16(1) of the FSS Act enumerates the duties and function of the Food Authority to regulate and monitor the manufacture, processing, distribution, sale and import of food as to ensure safe and wholesome food and Section 16(5) of the FSS Act stipulates that directions given by the Food Authority from time to time on matters relating to food safety and standards shall be binding upon the Commissioner of Food Safety.

Section 80 of the FSS Act provides for defences that may or may not be allowed in prosecution/adjudication under this Act and vide subsection (B)
of Section 80 FSS Act, the defence of due diligence is allowed to the effect of the defaulter proving taking of all reasonable precautions and exercise of due diligence to prevent the commission of the offence under the Act that is alleged to have been committed by that person or by another person under his control.

Defense of due diligence is allowed if the commission of offence happens due to act of default of another person or where the food item is sold in the same condition as it was purchased, then the offence of due diligence is allowed.

9. It is pertinent to mention that the Food Safety and Standards (Packaging & Labeling) Regulations,
2011 have been framed in exercised of powers under Section 92(2)(k) read with Section 23 of the FSS Act and Regulations 2.2 of FSS (P&L) Regulations, is about labelling requirements providing for general regulations with regard to prepackaged foods.

Lastly, we need to understand also that in terms of Food Safety and Standards (Food Products Standards and Food Additives) Regulations,
2011, vide Item No. 15.1 in AppendixA, 'Bhujiya' is classified as "savoury food".

Reverting to the instant matter, First thing first, there is considerable merit in the plea taken by Ld. sentences.text: This is clearly exemplified from a conjoint reading of Section 3(iii) and 43 of the FSS Act.

In this regard,
reference can be made to the cited case titled "Nestle India Ltd. Vs. The Food Safety and Standards Authority of India" (supra), wherein it was also held that it was incumbent in adjudication/prosecution under FSS Act that not only the food analyst but also the laboratory itself should be recognized and accredited by the Food Authority and since on that day when the samples were tested, the laboratory was not recognized and there was no accreditation to the competency of the food analyst under Section 45 of the FSS Act, and it was held that the said report cannot be relied upon.

sentences.text:
11. All said and done, the Ld. Chief Public Prosecutor for the respondent department was right in canvassing that de hor of lab analysis, the sampled item was a sheer case of misbranding in terms of Section 3(1) (zf) read with Section 3(1)(zf)(c) as it offered or promoted for sale an item with false or misleading claim and it's label failed to give a declaration with regard to artificial flavoring;
colouring or chemical preservatives, if any, used.

Having said that, this is the second aspect of the matter and Ld. Counsel for the appellants rightly relied upon the recommendations by FSSI Circular/Modification No.15 (28)/Advisory/RCD/FSSI dated 17.01.2020 whereby in continuation of previous clarification of letter dated 17.07.2018, it was advised that in cases of minor labeling defects without any food safety concern, 'improvement notice' be issued under Section 32 of FSS Act instead of initiating adjudication proceedings against the concerned Food Business Operator (FBO).
12.
The sum and substance of the aforesaid letter dated 17.01.2020 was that prosecution/adjudication in minor labeling defects result in sheer wastage of resources of the enforcement authority.

There was Annexure1 attached with the said letter dated 17.01.2020, which provided that if list of ingredients are not disclosed on the labels of the items that are in the nature of savouries, as also vide item No.5 if nutritional facts are not displayed on labels in relation to savouries, then by necessary implication instead of initiating adjudication proceedings improvement notice to be given under Section 32 of the FSS Act.
13.

Ld. Chief Public Prosecutor, however, referred to rule 2.2.2.2(c) whereby it is provided that the label must be containing the type of "vegetable or animal oil" used in the preparation of the food item and it was urged that in terms of rule 2.2.2.(10), there was no indication of "Best Before" or "use by date" in the seized samples item.

While former indeed was the case, Ld. Counsel for the appellants was right in canvassing that the seized sampled food item in the nature of savouries was governed by the recommendation of the FSSI, and in case of minor labeling defects that is not causing food safety concerns, improvement notice be given instead of long drawn adjudication.

The plea by the Ld. Chief Public Prosecutor that such advisory/recommendation was not binding is belied from the plain reading of section 16(5) of the FSS Act that categorically provides that directions on the matters of food safety and standards issued by the Food Authority of India are binding upon the Commissioner of Food (Safety).

sentences.text: Thirdly, this is a stark case where the benefit of Section 80(B) of FSS Act can be accorded to the appellants which accords recognition to the defence of due diligence since it is admitted case that appellant Nos.1 to 3 were suppliers of food items that were bought by them in terms of invoices by the suppliers/manufacturers vide Section 26(4) of FSS Act, and therefore, there is no doubt that the labeling part was done by the manufacturer and by virtue of Section 80B(2)(d)(1), the appellants cannot be held liable.
It, therefore, follows that appellant nos. 1, 2 & 3 had no reasons to suspect that the manufacturer had committed any act of omission that would constitute an offence under FSS Act.
There is no evidence of tempering with respect to the sample commodity which was being sold in the same packed state.

15. Having said that, the last question raised about violation of regulation No.2.2.2.(10) regarding "best before date", does not constitute an offence either as the packet of the sample clearly provided that "BEST BEFORE FOUR MONTHS" below the date of packaging and it is not fathomable that any consumer would be deceived by the said declaration.
Since, no 'improvement notice' was given to the appellant nos.4&5 as referred hereinabove, the whole proceedings against them are also non est in law.
FINAL ORDER 16.
In view of the foregoing discussions, the present appeal is allowed.
The impugned order dated 02.06.2021 whereby penalty has been imposed under Section 52 of FSS Act is hereby quashed.
The FD/DD filed by the appellants in terms of earlier order be released to them forthwith.
17. Record of the Ld. ADM along with copy of the judgment be sent back.
18. Appeal file be consigned to Record Room.
